headline: Unemployment among university graduates hits 13.54% in Bangladesh, highest across all education levels
summary: Around 885,000 university graduates in Bangladesh are jobless, facing daily struggles to cover living expenses and long waits for employment, leading to a significant loss of the country's demographic dividend.
details: A recent labor force survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) reveals a stark reality: the unemployment rate among university graduates in Bangladesh stands at 13.54%. This figure is the highest across all education levels, highlighting a significant challenge for the nation's educated youth.

The survey indicates that approximately 885,000 university graduates are currently jobless. In contrast, individuals with no formal education face a much lower unemployment rate of just 1.25%, suggesting that higher education degrees are increasingly associated with a greater risk of unemployment.

This statistic translates into daily struggles for many, like Asif, a former Jagannath University student living in Narinda, Old Dhaka, who worries about job prospects and rent two years post-graduation. Tanvir in Rajabazar faces similar challenges with commuting and daily expenses, while Roni from Rangpur, who travels to Dhaka for exams, has accumulated two months of unpaid mess rent and grocery bills.

Experts note that these individuals represent millions of unemployed youth. Annually, around 700,000 graduates enter the job market, but only about 300,000 institutional jobs are created. Furthermore, the public service commission (BPSC) shows that securing a final job recommendation can take three to five years, creating age and experience barriers for private sector entry.

Professor Ridwanul Hoque of Dhaka University's IBA identifies a key issue: the mismatch between educational qualifications and job market demands. He warns that institutional employment in fields like media and accounting will shrink in the age of AI, while technical skills will see increased demand.

To address this, he emphasizes the need to upgrade technical education to international standards and increase technology use. Young people are also advised to engage in internships, part-time jobs, or skill-based projects early on, rather than solely pursuing specific government or corporate roles for years.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) reports a 9.39% unemployment rate for youth aged 18-24 in Bangladesh. Economists from CPD and the World Bank estimate that billions of dollars are lost annually in GDP growth as the country fails to utilize its 'demographic dividend' due to a lack of suitable skills.

While policy reforms and curriculum changes are long-term solutions, thousands of young people in messes across the country are currently battling for monthly survival. The burden of mess rent and job application fees traps an entire generation's potential in a cycle of uncertainty.

topic: Teachers unpaid for decade continue teaching
headline_marked: [[10 teachers teach without pay for over a decade]] at Nasirnagar Chatalpar Degree College
headline: 10 teachers teach without pay for over a decade at Nasirnagar Chatalpar Degree College
summary: Despite not receiving salaries for 11 to 15 years due to lack of MPO enlistment, ten dedicated teachers at Chatalpar Degree College continue to educate students, relying on alternative income sources.
details: Ten dedicated teachers at Chatalpar Degree College in Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, have been teaching for 11 to 15 years without receiving any salary or benefits. Their struggle stems from the college's degree section not being included in the government's Monthly Pay Order (MPO) scheme.

Alfaz Uddin, a lecturer, supports his family by cultivating and selling vegetables like coriander, spinach, and eggplant on leased land. He joined the college in 2016, hoping for MPO enlistment, but has not received a single taka in salary since.

Alfaz needs 25,000 to 30,000 BDT monthly to run his family, forcing both him and his father to work in fields and markets. He expresses a sense of neglect and finds social invitations burdensome due to his financial struggles.

Similarly, Abdur Rashid, an Islamic studies teacher who joined in 2014, has also not received any salary for a decade. With his wife's single income as a primary school teacher being insufficient, he has had to sell land and now cultivates vegetables and tutors students.

Chatalpar Degree College was established in 1995 in a remote, riverine area of Nasirnagar. Out of 27 teachers at the institution, 17 receive MPO benefits, but the 10 teachers in the degree (pass) and certificate courses remain unpaid.

The college introduced BA (Pass) courses in 2011 and BSS (Pass) courses in 2015. Currently, approximately 550 students are enrolled across higher secondary and degree levels, with about 200 students in the degree section.

The college principal, Md. Omar Ali, stated that they have applied for MPO enlistment three times since the degree section began, but without success. He explained that the college's income is very limited, barely covering operational costs, making it impossible to pay the teachers.

Despite the teachers' dedication and the students' consistently satisfactory results in national university and education board exams, their long-standing efforts lack financial recognition. The college authorities recently approached the local MP, who has sent a demi-official letter to the relevant minister advocating for the MPO enlistment of the degree (pass) course.

These teachers continue to impart knowledge year after year without pay, driven by the hope that one day the college's degree section will be MPO-listed. They aspire for their teaching profession to become the primary source of livelihood for their families.
